title: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults and children with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) in Indian hospitals, built on the ICMR DKA workflow (July 2022), with the 2024 international consensus for HHS and resolution criteria and ISPAD 2022 for children.

pathophysiology.summary: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is caused by absolute or relative insulin deficiency with excess counter-regulatory hormones. Lipolysis releases free fatty acids that the liver turns into ketone bodies, producing a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, while unchecked hepatic glucose output and reduced uptake cause hyperglycaemia and an osmotic diuresis that depletes water, sodium and potassium. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) has enough insulin to suppress ketogenesis but not hyperglycaemia, so glucose and osmolality rise much higher with profound dehydration and little acidosis. In India DKA may be the first presentation of type 1 diabetes, and missed insulin, infection (fever, cough, loose stools, burning micturition) and SGLT2-inhibitor use are recognised triggers (ICMR STW 2022; 2024 consensus).
keyMechanisms: Insulin deficiency with high glucagon drives ketogenesis and acidosis.
Glucose above the renal threshold causes osmotic diuresis, dehydration and loss of total-body potassium.
Serum potassium can be normal or high at presentation despite total-body depletion; insulin moves potassium into cells.
In HHS, residual insulin prevents ketosis but severe hyperosmolality causes altered sensorium.
SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose (euglycaemic DKA).

symptoms: Symptoms of the trigger: fever, cough, loose stools, burning micturition (ICMR STW)
redFlags: pH below 7.0 or bicarbonate below 10 mEq/L, stupor or coma: severe DKA, admit to the intensive care unit (ICU) (ICMR STW)
Urine output below 30 mL/hour for 2 consecutive hours (ICMR STW)
Potassium below 3.3 mEq/L or electrocardiogram (ECG) changes before insulin (ICMR STW)
Children: headache, slowing heart rate or falling conscious level after treatment starts (cerebral oedema, ISPAD 2022)
HHS: effective osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg with altered sensorium
precipitants: Acute illness such as myocardial infarction, pancreatitis or stroke

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Glucose normal or low; history of alcohol or fasting.
High lactate with low or absent ketones.
Raised osmolar gap or salicylate level; history of ingestion.
Abdominal pain that persists after acidosis is corrected needs surgical review; raised amylase alone does not prove pancreatitis (ICMR STW).
Search for another cause of obtundation if osmolality is below 320 mOsm/kg (ICMR STW).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Glucose ≥200 mg/dL or known diabetes, AND beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥2+, AND pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L.
Mild: pH 7.25–7.3, bicarbonate 15–18, alert. Moderate: pH 7.0–7.25, bicarbonate 10–15, drowsy. Severe: pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10, stupor or coma — ICU.
Glucose ≥600 mg/dL, effective osmolality >300 mOsm/kg (or total >320), beta-hydroxybutyrate <3.0 mmol/L, pH ≥7.3 and bicarbonate ≥15 mmol/L.
Beta-hydroxybutyrate <0.6 mmol/L AND venous pH ≥7.3 or bicarbonate ≥18 mmol/L.
Osmolality <300 mOsm/kg, glucose <250 mg/dL, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h and improved cognition.
Glucose >11 mmol/L (about 200 mg/dL), venous pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L, and beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥3 mmol/L or moderate/large ketonuria.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and confirm
actions: Check airway, Glasgow Coma Scale score, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature and hydration (ICMR STW).
Send capillary glucose, ketones, venous blood gas, sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and ECG (ICMR STW).
Grade severity; severe DKA (pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10, stupor or coma) goes to the ICU (ICMR STW).
Start strict hourly input-output charting; report urine output below 30 mL/hour for 2 consecutive hours (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Fluids before insulin
actions: Adults: 1 L of 0.9% saline over the first hour, then 250–500 mL/hour (ICMR STW).
Never start insulin before intravenous fluids (ICMR STW pitfalls).
Older adults and patients with heart or kidney failure: use smaller boluses such as 250 mL and reassess (2024 consensus).
0.9% saline 10–20 mL/kg over 20–30 minutes; 20 mL/kg if perfusion is poor; then replace the deficit over 24–48 hours (ISPAD 2022).

clinicalManagement.title: Insulin and potassium
actions: Potassium below 3.3 mEq/L or ECG changes: give potassium first and hold insulin (ICMR STW).
Start insulin once potassium is safe; double the infusion if glucose falls by less than 10% in the first hour (ICMR STW).
Add potassium 10–20 mEq/hour to fluids once potassium is below 5.5 mEq/L and urine is flowing (ICMR STW).
When glucose falls below 250 mg/dL add 5% dextrose at 50 mL/hour and keep insulin running until ketoacidosis resolves (ICMR STW).
Insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour; glucose fall no more than 90–120 mg/dL/hour, sodium fall no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, osmolality fall 3–8 mOsm/kg/hour (2024 consensus).
Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor; children start dextrose immediately after initial volume expansion (ISPAD 2022).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor
actions: Vital signs and glucose every hour (ICMR STW).
Venous pH, sodium, potassium and bicarbonate every 2–4 hours (ICMR STW).
Ketones: ICMR suggests every 12 hours; the 2024 consensus checks beta-hydroxybutyrate every 4 hours where available.
Children: hourly neurological checks; treat suspected cerebral oedema immediately (ISPAD 2022).

clinicalManagement.title: Stop the infusion safely
actions: Stop intravenous insulin only when the patient is eating, glucose is consistently below 250 mg/dL, anion gap has normalised and acidosis is corrected (ICMR STW).
Give subcutaneous basal and short-acting insulin at least 30 minutes before stopping the infusion (ICMR STW).
Treat the trigger; educate on injection technique, glucose and ketone testing before discharge (2024 consensus).

pathophysiology.summary: A seizure is a transient episode of abnormal, excessive and synchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy is an enduring tendency to unprovoked seizures. Provoked seizures follow fever, an acute brain insult, drugs such as some antibiotics or metabolic causes and are treated by removing the cause (ICMR STW). Convulsive status epilepticus is a motor convulsion lasting more than 5 minutes with loss of consciousness and is a medical emergency: the longer seizures continue, the more GABA-A receptors are internalised, so benzodiazepines lose effect and neuronal injury, hyperthermia, acidosis and aspiration follow. Treatment is therefore time-staged — benzodiazepine first, then an intravenous antiseizure drug, then anaesthetic infusion in the intensive care unit (ICU) for refractory status (ICMR STW). In India neurocysticercosis, tuberculosis, alcohol and hypoglycaemia are causes to look for.
keyMechanisms: Imbalance between excitatory (glutamate) and inhibitory (GABA) transmission causes synchronous firing.
Prolonged seizures reduce GABA-A receptor numbers, so benzodiazepines work best early.
Ongoing convulsion causes hypoxia, acidosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and neuronal injury.
Structural (infection, stroke, tumour), metabolic and toxic causes provoke seizures and must be treated.

symptoms: Loss of consciousness or awareness, blank staring
Bizarre behaviour out of context (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Focal neurological deficit (suggests a structural cause)
redFlags: Convulsion lasting more than 5 minutes with loss of consciousness: status epilepticus (ICMR STW)
Fever, headache, vomiting, altered sensorium, severe giddiness or loss of bodily function (ICMR STW red flags)
Seizures after recent injury or an alcohol binge (ICMR STW)
No response to an adequate dose and duration of medication, or serious drug side effects (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Sleep deprivation, alcohol, photic stimulation (ICMR STW)

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilise
actions: Airway, breathing, circulation; oxygen; IV access; check glucose (ICMR STW).
Give thiamine before glucose if alcohol use is suspected (ICMR STW).
Time the seizure; inform the on-call consultant (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: First line: one benzodiazepine
actions: At home or before IV access: buccal or intranasal midazolam 0.3–0.5 mg/kg (ICMR STW).
In the emergency room: lorazepam, midazolam or diazepam IV (see medicines).

clinicalManagement.title: Second line: IV antiseizure drug
actions: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg at 50 mg/min; give a further 10 mg/kg if seizures continue after 15–20 minutes (ICMR STW).
If not controlled or phenytoin is contraindicated: IV valproate; if both are contraindicated: phenobarbitone and be ready to intubate (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Refractory status: ICU
clinicalManagement.timeframe: 60 minutes or after failure of 2 IV drugs
actions: Intubate and start an anaesthetic infusion with continuous EEG monitoring (ICMR STW).
Taper the infusion gradually after seizures stop, preferably guided by EEG (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Long-term epilepsy care
actions: Start one broad-spectrum antiseizure drug at a low dose ('start low, go slow') (ICMR STW).
Counsel on adherence, side effects, 7–8 hours of sleep, avoiding alcohol and photic stimulation, and a seizure diary (ICMR STW).
Avoid valproate and polytherapy in women of childbearing age; add folic acid 5 mg/day (ICMR STW).

branches.condition: Referral to district hospital or neurologist
actions: Progressive symptoms, recent injury, seizures after alcohol binge, status after stabilisation, no response to adequate treatment, serious side effects or need for imaging (ICMR STW).

teaching.scope: Seizures, epilepsy and convulsive status epilepticus in India.
learningObjectives: Recognise status epilepticus at 5 minutes and give one benzodiazepine.
Escalate to an IV antiseizure drug and then ICU care on time.
Choose safe long-term treatment, especially for women of childbearing age.
keyPoints: Treat at 5 minutes; do not wait.
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg at 50 mg/min; repeat 10 mg/kg once.
Avoid valproate in women of childbearing age; give folic acid 5 mg/day.
pitfalls: Repeated benzodiazepine doses without moving to second line.
Giving glucose before thiamine in alcohol use.
Starting valproate in liver disease or in children under 2 without specialist advice.

pathophysiology.summary: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is persistent, usually progressive airflow limitation caused by long-term inhalation of noxious particles. In India tobacco smoking is joined by smoke from cooking on solid fuels (wood, dung, crop waste) and occupational dust as major causes, so COPD is common in non-smoking women (ICMR STW). Inflammation narrows and remodels small airways and destroys alveolar walls (emphysema), causing air trapping, hyperinflation and breathlessness that worsens over years. Chronic hypoxia leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. Exacerbations — acute worsening of dyspnoea, sputum volume and purulence — are mostly triggered by viral or bacterial infection and drive decline and death. Diagnosis needs post-bronchodilator spirometry, and pulmonary tuberculosis must be excluded when cough lasts more than 2 weeks (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Chronic airway inflammation narrows small airways and increases mucus.
Alveolar destruction (emphysema) causes air trapping and hyperinflation.
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia and, in severe disease, hypercapnia.
Chronic hypoxia causes pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale and secondary polycythaemia.

symptoms: Exacerbations with more dyspnoea, sputum volume and purulence (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Barrel-shaped chest, hyper-resonant percussion, diminished breath sounds, rhonchi (ICMR STW)
Forced expiratory time above 6 seconds (ICMR STW)
Cor pulmonale: loud P2, raised jugular venous pressure, oedema (ICMR STW)
redFlags: Altered sensorium (ICMR STW)
SpO2 below 88% despite therapy (ICMR STW)
Heart rate above 110/min or systolic BP below 90 mmHg (ICMR STW)
Respiratory rate above 30/min, cyanosis, paradoxical breathing or asterixis (severe exacerbation, ICMR STW)
High-risk comorbidity: arrhythmia, heart failure, poorly controlled diabetes, renal or liver failure (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Onset in youth, variable symptoms, marked reversibility; see the ICMR Asthma STW comparison table.
Cough over 2 weeks, fever, weight loss, haemoptysis; sputum for acid-fast bacilli (ICMR STW).
Orthopnoea, raised jugular venous pressure, cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion on X-ray.
Daily copious purulent sputum; crackles; bronchial dilatation on computed tomography (CT).
Haemoptysis, weight loss, focal signs or abnormal chest X-ray (ICMR STW alternative-diagnosis flags).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70.
Mild: FEV1 above 80% predicted. Moderate: 50–79%. Severe: below 50% or complications (respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, secondary polycythaemia). The worst category decides severity.
Increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume and increased sputum purulence.
Any of: cyanosis, respiratory rate above 30/min, heart rate above 110/min, systolic BP below 90 mmHg, SpO2 below 90%, paradoxical breathing, altered sensorium, asterixis, severe comorbidity.

ruleIn.normalValue: FEV1/FVC 0.70 or above; FEV1 above 80% predicted
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Required in every provisionally diagnosed patient; refer if unavailable (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm and grade
actions: Suspect COPD in anyone over 35 with chronic cough or progressive breathlessness and smoke or dust exposure (ICMR STW).
Exclude tuberculosis when cough lasts more than 2 weeks (ICMR STW).
Confirm with post-bronchodilator spirometry; grade by FEV1, mMRC dyspnoea score, exacerbations and complications (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Stable COPD
actions: Stop smoking and reduce solid-fuel smoke exposure (ICMR STW).
Prescribe inhalers by severity (see medicines); check adherence and inhaler technique at every visit (ICMR STW).
Review every 3–6 months if mild or moderate, every 1–3 months if severe (ICMR STW).
Severe COPD: add tiotropium and/or a low-dose methylxanthine, or refer (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Exacerbation
actions: Increase bronchodilator dose or frequency; nebulise every 20 minutes as needed (ICMR STW).
Give a 5-day antibiotic and prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days (ICMR STW).
Severe exacerbation: oxygen to SpO2 92% (ICMR STW).
Refer to a higher centre with oxygen and nebulisation continued during transfer (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Admission and discharge
actions: Admit for severe or sudden dyspnoea at rest, falling saturation, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness, failure of initial treatment or serious comorbidity (ICMR STW).
Discharge when parameters are back to baseline, maintenance therapy is understood, acute drugs are complete and comorbidities are controlled; review 1 week after discharge (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a rapid fall in glomerular filtration shown by rising serum creatinine or falling urine output. Causes are pre-renal (low effective blood flow from hypotension, volume loss through vomiting, diarrhoea or bleeding, heat stroke, heart failure or decompensated liver disease), intrinsic renal (acute tubular injury from sepsis, nephrotoxic or indigenous drugs, plant and chemical toxins, radiocontrast, snake and other animal bites, haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis and pregnancy complications) and post-renal (urinary obstruction) (ICMR STW). Falling filtration causes retention of potassium, acid, fluid and urea, so hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, pulmonary oedema and uraemic encephalopathy or pericarditis are the life-threatening complications that may need dialysis. Many causes are reversible if recognised early, which is why ICMR stresses 'act fast, protect kidneys'.
keyMechanisms: Reduced renal perfusion lowers filtration (pre-renal) and, if prolonged, causes tubular injury.
Toxins, haem pigments, sepsis and venom injure tubules directly (intrinsic AKI).
Obstruction raises tubular pressure and stops filtration (post-renal).
Loss of excretion causes hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload and uraemia.

actions: Apply the AKI definition after excluding obstruction (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Preliminary actions
actions: Correct hydration; stabilise blood pressure; treat infection; optimise glucose (ICMR STW).
Stop nephrotoxic drugs, including ACE inhibitors and ARBs when potassium is high (ICMR STW).
Exclude and relieve urinary outflow obstruction (ICMR STW).
Monitor urine volume and body weight; look for complications (ICMR STW).
Give anti-snake venom and correct haemodynamics (ICMR STW).
Give the specific antidote if available (ICMR STW).
Manage the obstetric complication; deliver if indicated (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat hyperkalaemia
actions: Calcium gluconate under ECG monitoring, then salbutamol and insulin-dextrose (see medicines) (ICMR STW).

Urgent dialysis if life-threatening; potassium binders if dialysis is unavailable (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Level of care and referral
actions: Primary care: correct volume, stop nephrotoxins, relieve bladder obstruction, treat hyperkalaemia, IV loop diuretic and oxygen for pulmonary oedema, peritoneal dialysis if indicated, then refer (ICMR STW).

Tertiary care: kidney biopsy, multidisciplinary care, CRRT and plasma exchange where indicated (ICMR STW).

Check creatinine and urine protein every 6–12 months for life (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood at normal filling pressures, causing breathlessness, fatigue and fluid retention. In India the common causes are ischaemic cardiomyopathy after myocardial infarction, diabetic and hypertensive heart disease, rheumatic valvular disease, post-viral myocarditis, peripartum cardiomyopathy, idiopathic cardiomyopathy and cancer chemotherapy (ICMR STW). Reduced cardiac output activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and sympathetic systems; this retains salt and water and raises filling pressures, causing pulmonary and systemic congestion, while chronic neurohormonal activation remodels the ventricle and worsens function. Disease-modifying drugs block these pathways: angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor; diuretics relieve congestion but do not change prognosis. Heart failure is acute if under 3 months and chronic if over 3 months (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Low output activates renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and sympathetic systems.
Salt and water retention raises filling pressure and causes congestion.
Neurohormonal activation remodels the ventricle and worsens function over time.
Arrhythmia, ischaemia, infection, anaemia and uncontrolled blood pressure precipitate decompensation.

pathophysiology.summary: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is hyperglycaemia first recognised in pregnancy. Placental hormones (human placental lactogen, progesterone, cortisol) cause rising insulin resistance through the second and third trimesters; women whose beta cells cannot compensate develop hyperglycaemia. Maternal glucose crosses the placenta but insulin does not, so fetal hyperinsulinaemia causes macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, polyhydramnios and neonatal hypoglycaemia, and raises the risk of pre-eclampsia and stillbirth. South Asian women have a high risk, so India tests every pregnant woman with a single-step 75 g oral glucose load irrespective of the last meal, with a 2-hour plasma glucose of 140 mg/dL or more defining GDM (MoHFW 2018). Women with GDM carry a long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and need lifelong screening.
keyMechanisms: Placental hormones increase insulin resistance after mid-pregnancy.
Inadequate beta-cell compensation causes maternal hyperglycaemia.
Fetal hyperinsulinaemia causes macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia.
Underlying insulin resistance persists, raising later type 2 diabetes risk.

clinicalManagement.title: Universal testing
actions: Test every pregnant woman with 75 g glucose in about 300 mL water drunk within 5–10 minutes, fasting or not (MoHFW).
Read the 2-hour value on a plasma-calibrated glucometer (MoHFW).

clinicalManagement.title: Medical nutrition therapy
actions: Start nutrition therapy and 30 minutes of daily walking (MoHFW).
Three small meals and 2–3 snacks with complex carbohydrates; about 350 kcal/day extra in the second and third trimesters; avoid severe calorie restriction (MoHFW).
Recheck 2-hour post-meal glucose after 2 weeks; if below 120 mg/dL continue and check at least monthly (MoHFW).

clinicalManagement.title: Insulin or metformin
actions: Insulin is first line and can start at any gestation (MoHFW).
Metformin only after 20 weeks if nutrition therapy fails (MoHFW).
Check fasting and 2-hour glucose every third day and titrate in 2-unit steps (MoHFW).
Refer if insulin exceeds 20 units/day or metformin 2 g/day, or any referral criterion is met (MoHFW).

clinicalManagement.title: Surveillance and delivery
actions: Teach daily fetal movement counting: 10 movements in 2 hours after a meal lying on the side (MoHFW).
Well-controlled GDM: deliver in a facility; induce at or after 39 weeks if not in labour (MoHFW).
Uncontrolled GDM: refer at 34–36 weeks to a CEmOC centre (MoHFW).
Vaginal birth preferred; consider caesarean at 39 weeks if estimated fetal weight is above 4 kg (MoHFW).
Withhold the morning insulin or metformin; glucose every 2 hours; normal saline 100 mL/hour with insulin added by glucose level (MoHFW).

clinicalManagement.title: After birth
actions: Breastfeed early; check the baby's glucose within 1 hour (MoHFW).
75 g OGTT at 6 weeks postpartum; if normal, annual screening and lifestyle advice at the NCD clinic (MoHFW).

pathophysiology.summary: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding arises proximal to the ligament of Treitz and presents with haematemesis, blood in the nasogastric aspirate or melaena. In India the two main groups are non-variceal bleeding — mostly peptic ulcers linked to NSAIDs, aspirin, antiplatelets and anticoagulants — and variceal bleeding from portal hypertension in cirrhosis, often from alcohol or chronic hepatitis B or C (ICMR STW). Ulcer bleeding comes from erosion into a submucosal artery; acid impairs clot stability, so high-dose proton pump inhibitor (PPI) helps. Variceal bleeding is driven by high portal pressure, which vasoconstrictors such as terlipressin, somatostatin or octreotide lower; cirrhotic patients who bleed are also prone to infection. Rapid loss causes hypovolaemic shock, so early resuscitation, risk assessment and endoscopy within 24 hours are the core of care (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Peptic ulcer erodes a submucosal vessel; acid destabilises the clot.
Portal hypertension dilates gastro-oesophageal varices that rupture under pressure.
Antiplatelets, anticoagulants and NSAIDs precipitate and worsen bleeding.
Blood loss causes hypovolaemia, tachycardia, hypotension and syncope.

pathophysiology.summary: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is usually caused by gut bacteria — mainly Escherichia coli — ascending the urethra. Infection confined to the bladder in an afebrile patient is uncomplicated cystitis; infection extending beyond the bladder or with systemic illness (fever, flank pain, rigors, haemodynamic instability) is complicated UTI or pyelonephritis (ICMR STW). Stones, obstruction, congenital anomalies, immunosuppression, pregnancy, chronic kidney disease and recent instrumentation make infection complicated (ICMR STW). In India, resistance to fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins among E. coli is common, so national guidelines favour nitrofurantoin for cystitis and culture-guided treatment of complicated infection. Asymptomatic bacteriuria needs treatment only in pregnancy or before urological procedures; routine culture of uncomplicated or asymptomatic patients is discouraged (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Ascending infection by bowel organisms, mainly Escherichia coli.
Bladder mucosal inflammation causes dysuria, frequency and urgency.
Spread to the kidney causes fever, flank pain and bacteraemia (pyelonephritis).
Obstruction, stones, catheters and immunosuppression impair clearance and cause complicated infection.

clinicalManagement.title: Classify
actions: Confirm symptoms; look for fever, flank pain, red flags and high-risk groups (ICMR STW).
Uncomplicated: treat without culture. Complicated or red flags: urine and blood culture, imaging if needed, urology referral if obstructed (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Symptom relief for all
actions: Plenty of water; urinary alkaliniser; paracetamol for pain (ICMR STW).
Phenazopyridine 200 mg three times daily for 2 days (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Choose the antibiotic pathway
actions: Uncomplicated cystitis: short oral course (see medicines).
Complicated UTI or pyelonephritis: parenteral start, then oral or IV by severity; 10–14 days for pyelonephritis, 7–10 days for lower UTI; adjust to culture (ICMR STW).
Prostatitis: treat as complicated UTI for 2–4 weeks; urology evaluation (ICMR STW).
Culture at the first antenatal visit; treat asymptomatic bacteriuria; for recurrent UTI give nitrofurantoin 50 mg or cephalexin 250 mg at bedtime until term (ICMR STW).
Do not test asymptomatic catheterised patients; remove the catheter as soon as possible; treat symptomatic infection as complicated UTI and change the catheter; no routine prophylaxis (ICMR STW).

Infants under 3 months: IV antibiotics as pyelonephritis (ICMR STW). Others: oral third-generation cephalosporin or co-amoxiclav for febrile UTI 7–10 days; IV only if under 2 months, very ill or vomiting (ISPN 2023).

clinicalManagement.title: Recurrent UTI
actions: Post-coital voiding with a single post-coital antibiotic dose, or 6 months of low-dose prophylaxis (nitrofurantoin 50 mg, co-trimoxazole 400/80 mg or cephalexin 250 mg); vaginal oestrogen after menopause (ICMR STW).
Complicated recurrent UTI: urology referral, cystoscopy and urodynamics (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. In children aged 2–59 months in India, common sources are pneumonia, diarrhoea, skin and soft-tissue infection, meningitis, and tropical infections such as malaria and dengue (ICMR STW). Inflammatory mediators cause vasodilation, capillary leak and myocardial depression, so the child develops tachycardia, cold peripheries, weak pulses and capillary refill longer than 3 seconds before blood pressure falls — hypotension is a late sign in children. Untreated shock leads to multi-organ failure. The ICMR pathway is rapid triage by perfusion, oxygen, antibiotics within 1 hour, 20 mL/kg fluid boluses with careful reassessment for fluid overload, adrenaline for persistent shock, and early referral to a centre with intensive care (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Infection triggers a systemic inflammatory response with vasodilation and capillary leak.
Reduced effective circulating volume and myocardial depression cause poor perfusion.
Compensatory tachycardia and vasoconstriction keep blood pressure normal until late.
Ongoing hypoperfusion causes organ dysfunction: altered consciousness, oliguria, respiratory failure.

symptoms: Fever with or without rash; pneumonia or diarrhoea (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Tachycardia: above 180/min under 12 months, above 120/min over 12 months (ICMR STW)

Hepatomegaly, falling SpO2 or new crepitations during fluids: stop fluids (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Pneumonia, diarrhoea, skin and soft-tissue infection (ICMR STW)

clinicalManagement.title: Triage by perfusion
actions: Check AVPU, pulse volume, heart and respiratory rate, capillary refill, SpO2 and blood pressure for age (ICMR STW).
Good perfusion: admit or treat per IMNCI. Poor perfusion: admit, treat and refer to a centre with an intensive care unit (ICU), ventilation and 24-hour monitoring if needed (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Oxygen, access, antibiotics
actions: Oxygen by face mask 4–6 L/min or hood 8–10 L/min (nasal prongs 1–2 L/min if unavailable); target SpO2 above 95% (ICMR STW).
Insert two IV cannulas; give the first antibiotic dose within 1 hour (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Fluid boluses for shock
actions: Normal saline 20 mL/kg over 20–30 minutes; repeat 20 mL/kg over 30 minutes (ICMR STW).
Stop fluids if hepatomegaly, falling SpO2 or chest crepitations appear (ICMR STW).
Suspected heart disease: give boluses cautiously (ICMR STW).

branches.condition: Hypovolaemic shock with diarrhoea that improves after the first bolus
actions: Give 70 mL/kg over 5 hours in infants or 2.5 hours in older children, plus ongoing losses (ICMR STW).
Start maintenance fluids (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Persistent shock and complications
actions: Start adrenaline infusion and refer to a higher centre (ICMR STW).
Respiratory failure (rising respiratory rate or SpO2 not above 94% on oxygen): CPAP, BiPAP or ventilation (ICMR STW).
Heart failure: dobutamine or milrinone with furosemide (ICMR STW).
Shock not improving after the second bolus, fluid overload or no continuous monitoring; counsel parents and inform the receiving centre (ICMR STW).

pathophysiology.summary: Antenatal care aims to keep mother and baby healthy, detect complications early and plan a safe institutional birth. Pregnancy raises plasma volume more than red-cell mass, increases iron and folate needs, and shifts metabolism towards insulin resistance; in India anaemia, hypertensive disorders, gestational diabetes and infections remain leading causes of maternal and perinatal harm. The ICMR workflow sets out at least four contacts — the first ideally in the first trimester, then the second trimester, 28–34 weeks and 36–40 weeks — with defined history, examination, tests, supplements (folic acid, iron-folic acid, calcium with vitamin D, deworming), tetanus-diphtheria (Td) immunisation, counselling on danger signs and birth preparedness, and referral of high-risk pregnancies to a district hospital or medical college (ICMR STW 2025).
keyMechanisms: Plasma volume expansion and higher iron demand cause anaemia if stores are low.
Placental hormones increase insulin resistance in later pregnancy.
Abnormal placentation underlies pre-eclampsia and growth restriction.
Folate deficiency around conception raises neural tube defect risk.

symptoms: Quickening and fetal movements from mid-pregnancy
Excessive vomiting or vaginal bleeding need assessment (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Weight and BMI; pallor; pedal oedema (ICMR STW)
Blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature
redFlags: Vaginal bleeding: examine per abdomen and speculum and refer to CHC or higher (ICMR STW)
Severe headache, blurred vision or convulsions (ICMR STW)
Reduced or absent fetal movements after 28 weeks (ICMR STW)
Leaking fluid, fever, breathlessness at rest, reduced urine or burning micturition, generalised itching (ICMR STW)
Haemoglobin below 7 g/dL: refer (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Age above 35 or below 19 years; parity above 4 (ICMR STW)
BMI below 18.5 or above 30 kg/m² (ICMR STW)
Previous caesarean, PPH or obstetric complication (ICMR STW)
Medical illness: diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, TB, epilepsy (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Early pregnancy with pain or bleeding; refer urgently.
Persistent vomiting with dehydration (danger sign, ICMR STW).
BP above 140/90 mmHg on two readings 6 hours apart with or without proteinuria (ICMR STW high-risk).
More than 4 weeks: wrong dates, growth restriction, multiple pregnancy or polyhydramnios (ICMR STW).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Medical illness, previous caesarean, past obstetric complication or congenital malformation, past PPH, age above 35 or below 19, parity above 4, BMI below 18.5 or above 30, haemoglobin below 7 g/dL, BP above 140/90 mmHg twice 6 hours apart, APH, fundal height discrepancy above 4 weeks, GDM or overt diabetes, multiple pregnancy, malpresentation at term, previous uterine surgery.
One IFA tablet daily if haemoglobin above 11 g%; two daily if below 11 g%.
Non-adherent or haemoglobin below 9 g/dL in the third trimester: iron sucrose; haemoglobin below 7 g/dL: refer.
24 weeks at the umbilicus; 36 weeks at the xiphisternum; 12 weeks just palpable above the symphysis.

clinicalManagement.title: First visit
actions: History: LMP and EDD, parity, complaints, medical and family history, consanguinity, tobacco and alcohol (ICMR STW).
Examination: height, weight, BMI, pallor, oedema, vital signs, thyroid, breasts, chest, heart, abdomen; speculum and vaginal examination (ICMR STW).
Register: Mother and Child Protection card, RCH portal entry and number; give the Safe Motherhood booklet (ICMR STW).
Start folic acid; give the first Td dose (or a single booster if a first dose was given within 3 years) (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Second visit
actions: Ask about quickening, fetal movements and adherence; check weight, pallor, oedema, BP, fundal height and fetal heart (ICMR STW).
Start IFA and calcium with vitamin D (never taken together); single albendazole 400 mg; second Td dose at least 4 weeks after the first (ICMR STW).
Refer if haemoglobin does not rise after 4 weeks of oral iron (ICMR STW).
Discuss birth preparedness (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Third and fourth visits
actions: Record gestation, fetal heart, abdominal girth and symphysio-fundal height (ICMR STW).
Continue IFA and calcium; iron sucrose if non-adherent or haemoglobin below 9 g/dL; refer if below 7 g/dL (ICMR STW).
Refer for fundal height–dates discrepancy or any danger sign (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Counselling and birth preparedness
actions: Next visit timing by risk; rest, balanced diet and exercise; HIV testing; danger signs; institutional delivery; exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months; postpartum contraception (ICMR STW).
Plan the delivery facility, birth companion, emergency transport with a phone number and blood donors (ICMR STW).
Antenatal care and delivery at a district hospital or medical college (ICMR STW).
